questions.knowledge_point: Improper Integral Involving Other Exponential Functions
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int {b}^{\,px+q}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{p\operatorname{ln}⁡(b)}{b}^{\,px+q}+C
$$

We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{5}^{x/2}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}{5}^{x/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{2\cdot {5}^{x/2}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[{5}^{x/2}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }(1-{5}^{a/2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\cdot (1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{5}^{a/2})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y={5}^{x/2}$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }{5}^{x/2}=0$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{5}^{x/2}=\infty $

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14056962/assets/141d1745dc939ca63155ca3313257f385af6d3c505c16bd63ba3b91e1e0ba64b.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{5}^{x/2}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\cdot (1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{5}^{a/2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\cdot (1-0) \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Improper Integral Using a Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=\sqrt{x}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\,⟹\,2\text{d}u=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=\sqrt{x}$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{6}^{-2\sqrt{x}}}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{6}^{-2u}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{6}^{-2\sqrt{x}}}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{6}^{-2u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{6}^{-2u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{{6}^{-2u}}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡6}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{6}^{-2u}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{6}^{2a}}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\frac{1}{{6}^{2x}},$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{6}^{2x}}=\infty $

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{{6}^{2x}}=0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14056962/assets/8f732515dd376db40889706419781e02cbedfcd4da8513a09e4f2d77ff88ece2.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{6}^{-2\sqrt{x}}}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{6}^{2a}}-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}\cdot (0-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Improper Integral Using a Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=\frac{1}{x}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to -\infty $ when $x\to {0}^{-}$ and $u\to 0$ when $x\to -\infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=\frac{1}{x}$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $-\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-\infty $ | $0$ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{3/x}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{0}^{-\infty }{e}^{3u}\,\text{d}u={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{e}^{3u}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{3/x}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}{e}^{3u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{{e}^{3u}}{3}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(1-{e}^{3a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{3a})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y={e}^{3x}$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }{e}^{3x}=0$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{e}^{3x}=\infty $

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14056962/assets/34abda46dc9fc2c6f14ce4f8460ba076a16004bb9141eb8074cdc08e0c12fd2f.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{3/x}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}(1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{3a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
